Boardy AI · Intro Matching
How the project unfolded
Recommender Systems · Boardy AI

Can we tell which introductions people will actually accept?

The findings that mattered, in the order they changed what we believed.

July 16 — August 13, 2026
01  ·  Framing

Every pair was already recommended. The label is what humans did next.

A hundred accepted. A hundred declined. The negatives are production’s own false positives — plausible intros people still walked away from. And whatever we build must answer in under 100 ms.

The task

Not topical relevance. Residual fit: will these two actually connect.

02  ·  Lexical floor

Plain keyword overlap already gets you about halfway — then stalls.

Query↔match lexical overlap looks almost the same for accepts and declines. TF-IDF cosine lands near ~0.59 and plateaus, because both classes already cleared production’s relevance bar.

What that means

If a model only measures topic overlap, it is solving yesterday’s problem.

Holdout baselines Local table
03  ·  Baselines

First we measured what already existed.

Frozen BERT was near chance. Voyage-4-nano did better. Voyage-4-large — Boardy’s production embedder — set the bar. Nothing gets called a win until it beats these, under the latency budget.

The decision

Accuracy alone is not enough. Serving must stay under 100 ms.

Matched holdout browser Embedding space
04  ·  Query ablation

Remove the search query and Voyage gets worse.

BERT barely noticed — it wasn’t using the ask anyway. Both Voyage models dropped on retrieval. The query is only ~2% of the seeker string, but it carries the ask that the biography dilutes.

Foreshadow

This becomes the project’s strongest lever — but only after we measure it properly on all 200.

05  ·  Synthetic generation

Two hundred real outcomes is not much to learn from.

So we built a pipeline that invents people and labeled intros overnight — hundreds of practice pairs, reviewed lightly, then promoted for training.

The bet

If we cannot buy more human outcomes, manufacture practice ones.

06  ·  LoRA run_001

The first fine-tune looked brilliant. It wasn’t.

Train-dev pair AUC near 0.99. On the real holdout: ~0.58 overall, and hard-negative AUC below chance. Worse than a coin flip on the cases production actually gets wrong.

The decision

Stop shipping numbers. Find what it really learned.

07  ·  Root cause

It read our handwriting, not human behaviour.

A classifier shown only the candidate’s profile guessed the synthetic label at 99.2% accuracy — and chance on real data. Arm A, trained on real pairs only, beat the synth-trained run with a fifth of the data.

The decision

Quarantine the batch. Never let the answer touch the text again.

08  ·  Safer generation

Invent the people first. Decide the match later.

Unlabeled profiles from Ollama and Bedrock — no pos/neg attached at write time. Pairing and judging became a separate step, so the generator could not smuggle the answer into the prose.

The invariant

Never let the label author the biography.

Pairs comparison graph Local graph
09  ·  LLM judge

Ask a model directly — and never give it the search query.

Gemini flash-lite beat Voyage-large on accept/decline, and uniquely did better on hard negatives than easy ones. That inversion is the tell: it is not scoring keyword overlap. Too slow to serve. Valuable as a labeler and distillation target.

Constraint

Per-candidate LLM calls are out under 100 ms. Keep the signal; move it into a bi-encoder.

Judge vs baselines Local comparison Prompt evolution
10  ·  Embeddings

A free model seemed to beat production. Then we checked on all 200.

On the 69-pair holdout, Qwen3-Embedding-8B looked like a breakthrough. On the full 200 real pairs the claim reversed — Voyage still wins overall. The holdout ranks broken models well and strong ones almost at random.

Retracted · Jul 31

All-200 is the canonical leaderboard. No open-weight model beats Voyage overall; BGE-en-ICL is closest on retrieval.

All-200 baseline sweep Local writeup 200-pair eval
11  ·  RRF pairing

Find with one family. Judge with another.

Dense + BM25 fused with RRF, then an LLM judge — so retrieval never grades its own ranking. Leakage probes dropped from catastrophic to merely cautious. The live weakness: some seekers are always rejected, so seeker identity alone predicts labels.

How to train

Within a seeker — comparisons that cancel base rate — not a plain pairwise classifier.

Triplet fine-tune Big-batch follow-up Ablation verdict
12  ·  Training recipe

One person, one good match, one bad match — many at once.

Triplet / contrastive training with a real corpus for checkpoint selection produced the best MRR in the project. Sharpening the loss to chase recall@1 backfired. Micro-batch size moved retrieval; an extra negative often hurt.

What held

Comparison learning under the latency budget beats isolated pair labels.

Top-1 optimised Qwen big-batch Local writeup
13  ·  Synth transfer

Safer generation fixed the handwriting leak. It did not fix the transfer gap.

Models trained on judge-labeled synthetic pairs still struggle to move real numbers. Synthetic vocabulary can transfer; synthetic labels often teach the teacher. A 25k-pair Qwen-judged batch showed the same seeker-identity leak, louder at scale. Scoring each lookingFor ask separately helped — the clever mixer less so.

Still open

Useable synth labels, distillation of the judge, and a real latency benchmark.

MoE on synth labels Sectioned MoE lookingFor sectioning
14  ·  Query-weighted

The biography was drowning the ask. Separate them, and recall nearly doubles.

On frozen voyage-4-nano with no training, encode query and profile apart, then blend: all-200 recall@1 goes 0.18→0.30, recall@10 0.59→0.91. Serving cost drops — online encode ~55 tokens instead of ~2,500. Name leakage ruled out; hard-neg AUC 0.5914 is the best of any model on all 200 so far.

The lever

What you feed the encoder at inference matters more than most of the training tricks we tried.

Query-weighted encoding Local writeup
15  ·  Fine-tune + query

The same pattern holds on the best fine-tune.

On top1_ctrl, query-only hits MRR 0.51 / R@1 0.32 — best retrieval of any model in the project. Alpha 0.6 hits pair AUC 0.6129 — best classification on all 200. Profile-only is weakest again: the biography dilutes, even after LoRA.

No extra latency

Cache the profile offline. Encode only the live query. Same serving shape as concat.

Query-weighted two-tower Topology graph
16  ·  Representation

Retraining on a special seeker text does not beat just using that text at eval.

No-query training lands within noise of eval-time profile-only on the normal adapter. Query-only training mirrors the same story. Voyage-4-large’s query-only arm is the best result of any model on all 200: R@1 0.42, MRR 0.59, hard-neg AUC 0.614. Native 2048-dim embeddings do not beat the usual 1024-dim truncation.

The lesson

The adapter’s usefulness is what you ask it to encode at inference — not training specialization.

No-query + large sweep Local writeup
17  ·  Funnel

Good at top-1, weak at AUC? That model belongs near the top of the stack.

Retrieval finds a shortlist. Classification decides accept vs decline. A strong R@1 with a soft AUC is a candidate-generation (or light-rank) win — not the final yes/no layer.

Rule of thumb

Put Voyage-style query retrieval up top. Keep AUC-strong judges or rankers for the decision.

18  ·  Split & gate

Two towers. A learned field gate. Both lost to one shared model plus the right text.

A genuinely split two-tower (separate LoRAs per role) was the worst of the query-only variants — hard-neg below chance. A learned gate over query / lookingFor / positioning was the worst of four on every retrieval metric. Holdout numbers looked great both times and reversed on all 200.

Conclusion

Added architecture has not beaten choosing what text to feed one shared tower.

Split two-tower Field gate Local split Local gate
19  ·  Alpha & sections

Calibrate the blend on synthetic data. Hard negatives still want more query.

On 2,619 synthetic pairs, alpha climbs to pure query. On real pairs, overall AUC peaks around 0.6 — but hard-neg AUC keeps climbing to 1.0. Blending the query with the closest lookingFor section beats whole-profile blending in the interior — a win the calibration curve cannot see, because synth pair-AUC is monotonic to the boundary.

Practical take

For the residual hard-neg task, lean query-heavy. Section-aware blending is a free interior gain.

Nomad drift Sectioned blend Local drift Local sectioned
20  ·  Prompt evolution

Ten automatic attempts at a smarter judge prompt. Naive still wins.

Hand-designed calibrated and structured CoT already lost. Auto-optimization grew rules, shrunk them, repaired contracts, swapped optimizers. Best clean run (evo_006) hit 0.6105 — still under naive’s 0.6177. The tenth run, seeded from the stronger focused prompt, lost the widest gap yet: it kept the yes/no and killed what “confidence” meant.

Ten ways, same answer

Manual, structured, and automatic — none beat four plain paragraphs.

Judge prompt evolution
21  ·  Field selection

Train on the ask, not the biography — and it beats the full-profile fine-tune.

A 105-way field sweep found the best frozen combo: seeker = search query only, candidate = background + lookingFor. Training that combo beat top1_ctrl on every metric. Hard-neg AUC 0.6564 — first embedding model to invert hard/easy like the LLM judge. Two-field identity trains all lost on ranking, and won only on hard-neg resistance.

The win is narrow

Keep the seeker’s ask. Trim the candidate to what they offer. Don’t strip both sides to identity fields.

Query-only + bg/look Field-pair trains
22  ·  Reciprocal matching

Score what they want from you, too.

Adding the candidate’s lookingFor against the seeker’s background lifts frozen-nano AUC on every population — directionally, not proven (bootstrap CIs cross zero). Fitting λ on synthetic labels collapsed to ~0. Sweeping λ without fitting shows a real positive-sided curve. Two dedicated Ask/Offer towers added reciprocal signal on all-200 (+0.059) but the forward tower itself was weaker than one shared encoder.

Cheap rerank, not a new tower

A shared model plus a free λ sweep still beats two jointly-trained towers.

Static reciprocal λ sweep Ask / Offer train
23  ·  Matrix factorization

Compress the words. Do not factor the people.

Classic LSA on the documents×terms matrix lifts hard-neg AUC on both TF-IDF and Voyage — a plateau, not a lucky rank. A learned bilinear correction on frozen embeddings fails at 131 training pairs: inner CV invented 0.74, honest out-of-fold was 0.62. Retrieval collapsed. Third experiment to hit this wall after the MoE reranker and the triplet ablation.

At this data size

Hyperparameter search is itself enough overfitting to invent a result.

LSA vs bilinear
24  ·  Scale

More synthetic data moved the needle. Qwen set the records. Treat the leakage.

Retraining top1_ctrl on a 5× larger, leakier batch beat it on every all-200 metric. A KL leash to the frozen base lost again, by a wider margin. Qwen3-8B on the same rows hit pair AUC 0.6446 and hard-neg 0.6862 — tying the LLM judge on classification, without a field-selection trick. Nano still wins retrieval. Candidate-only AUC on that batch was 0.758 before any training.

Asterisk

Headline numbers wait on a cleaner batch before they count as settled.

Nano on the new batch Qwen records KL still loses
25  ·  B-data

On Boardy’s actual production dump, nothing we already knew still works.

18k resolved ACCEPT/REJECT pairs, ~30k unique people. TF-IDF pair AUC 0.512 — chance. Frozen voyage-4-nano 0.469 — below chance; REJECT slightly more similar than ACCEPT. Narrowing to lookingFor+query vs positioning+background barely clears chance (0.518) and ranks the accepted person at median 184 of 21k.

The exam changed

The 200-pair seed set was a different, easier population. B-data is now the real test.

B-data summary TF-IDF on B-data Nano on B-data Ask / offer packing ~30k people
Where it stands · August 13

What we can say out loud.

The 200-pair seed taught us the levers. B-data is the exam.
Hard negatives are the whole population. All-200 ranks strong models on the seed. Frozen nano and TF-IDF are at or below chance on the production dump.
What you encode still beats a fancier tower.
Query-only + offer fields is the best trained recipe on the seed. Reciprocal is a cheap rerank. Ask/Offer towers and bilinear heads did not pay rent. LSA compression did.
Qwen on the leakier batch ties the judge — with an asterisk.
Pair AUC 0.6446, hard-neg 0.6862. Candidate-only leakage was 0.758 before training. Naive judge prompts still beat every evolved one.
Useable synthetic labels, a B-data model, and a latency number remain open.
Handwriting leak is fixed by construction. Teaching real outcomes from judge labels is not. Nothing has been timed under 100 ms.
